speakeroldname: Mr. Ray Skelly (North Island -Powell River) moved:
subtopic: PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should demonstrate to Canadians that Members of Parliament and their support staff are subject to the same regulations enforced in federal buildings with regard to the smoking of tobacco products by banning immediately all smoking of tobacco products on Parliament Hill.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise in the House to speak today on this important issue.
The issue comprises two things. One is the matter of a very serious health problem in Canada, indeed the world, and that is smoking and consumption of tobacco products. There is the impact on our health budget and on our population, generally.
The second aspect of it is the question of the House of Commons adhering to regulations that it has put forward, as well as setting an example for the rest of the country.
By the end of this Private Members' Hour, I would ask if the Chair will be ruling on a matter raised by the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants. He had made a plea, in a question of privilege, that smoking by members
of the Conservative caucus on the other side in the lobby be curtailed or ended as per the requirements.
The motion that we are dealing with today, in attempting to curtail or at least prohibit smoking entirely on Parliament Hill, is very relevant. It asks that members of Parliament set an example by following the rules that they have laid down, especially in an area such as the House of Commons. It would be my hope that the Chair would take this very timely opportunity to answer that particular question of privilege and whether or not the rules and regulations imposed by the House will in fact in this place, the House of Commons, be followed.
The second thing that I would be asking today, probably by the same vehicle, is that the Speaker's office become involved in the matter of enforcement of the regulations of the House. The maintenance staff of the House of Commons report that 20 per cent of the offices are still permitting smoking to be carried on in the offices on the Hill. Apparently, they have kept a survey of offices in the simple matter of clearing out the ashtrays. The rules are not being adhered to. It would be my hope that, at the end of the day, that matter would be dealt with as well by the Speaker's office in an attempt to encourage members, support staff, and employees on Parliament Hill to follow through on it.
Why? It is a simple matter. If the House treats with contempt rules and regulations to attempt to preserve and enhance the health of Canadians, surely nobody else has to follow them. When I walk along beside a school yard, be it in British Columbia or as far away as Brookfield High School here in Ottawa, and see hundreds of young people in front of those schools smoking, I think we have an obligation as people in elected office to set an example to carry that out.
The thrust of this motion asks that there be no smoking on Parliament Hill, period. The reason for this is twofold: It is a serious health problem and there is a need for an example.
Hopefully, the question of privilege will be picked up today and the Speaker's office will treat as a serious

October 29, 1990

matter that still about 20 per cent of the offices pay absolutely no heed to the question of smoking on the Hill.
The third item is that the gatherings at the doors are just intolerable. There are rights for people who do not smoke and those individuals who do should be moved off Parliament Hill if they intend to smoke.
The question of smoking is an interesting one. I would like to begin the main body of my remarks by quoting from a hearing of the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment of the House of Representatives in the United States in July of 1988.
The matter before the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment in the House of Representatives revealed a document from the research department of Philip Morris by William L. Dunn, a researcher for them. He said we should understand clearly that "cigarettes should not be conceived of as a product", but that Philip Morris uses cigarettes only as a package to sell a drug, nicotine. The report states the product of this tobacco company is nicotine, and the cigarette and the other forms in which it is sold are simply the packaging. The report states:
The cigarette is but one of many packaged layers. Think of the
cigarettes pack as a storage container for a day's supply of nicotine.
Think of cigarettes as a dispenser for a dose unit of nicotine, think
of a puff of smoke as the vehicle for nicotine.
In short, before the American Subcommittee on Health and the Environment, it was clearly defined by the company itself that it was in the business of selling drugs. We in the House of Commons have got to adopt that approach to this product. In fact, the drug is defined as one that is more addictive than heroin.
It is ironic that there is not a smoker who does not say: "I want to quit, " and that smokers do not believe that this activity is a healthy activity. They are convinced by the information that it is detrimental to their health and they want to quit. Unfortunately, there is not an incentive that brings them to want to quit right now.
We have that opportunity on the Hill to clean up the act, in the government lobby by answering a question of privileges, and in the offices of members of Parliament by addressing this report from maintenance that says 20
per cent of the offices are still permitting smoking. That should happen and that should happen today.
The next point is that the health budget of Canada in 1987 ran something in the order of $46 billion. It was estimated that up to 5 per cent of that was treating people who voluntarily damage their health or the health of others by consumption of tobacco and smoking. It is interesting that we are talking in the order of $2 billion to $3 billion of the health budget expended in treating illnesses that are completely preventable, caused by a voluntary activity. If smoking stopped that area of illness that would disappear. Those health care resources could certainly be better used in treating children with cystic fibrosis, in expanding health care technology, and in community health programs. There are 1,001 areas, such as reducing the waiting lists in British Columbia for coronary artery transplants and open heart surgery that will save lives. This squandering of health care resources is a terrible situation.
The Parliament of Canada has an opportunity to set an example. Not only do we see that this is not enforced in the members' lobbies, this is not enforced in members' offices, and employees are permitted to smoke on the Hill. We have a nursing staff which operates health units on the Hill. Those health units do not have a statement of goals and objectives aimed at trying to assist people on the Hill who smoke to stop.
Mark my words, there is not a smoker who does not want to get out from under this habit. The consumption of nicotine is as powerful, if not more powerful, than heroin. The nurses on the Hill are a competent and committed staff, who do not have a set of objectives laid out for them by the human resources operation and who do not know how many people smoke on the Hill, who do not in any regular way offer quit-smoking courses, and who do not follow up. In an interview with the nursing staff, they indicated that there needs to be a budget allocation for that kind of activity. There needs to be a steady follow-up of how many people are smoking, how many people have tried to quit smoking and, again, a substantial, working, quit-smoking operation on this Hill that is an example to other industries and other operations in Canada. Rather than being in the back eddy of this activity, we should be leading it and setting an example for others to follow. The argument was that
October 29, 1990

there was not enough, in terms of human resources, to undertake that kind of study.
At Algonquin College and at the University of Ottawa, there are student nursing programs in which part of their practicum is to undertake public health assignments. This assignment of undertaking a survey on Parliament Hill, assisting in setting up quit-smoking operations and doing some follow-up would be an excellent public health practicum for those nursing students of Algonquin College or the University of Ottawa. It is simply a matter of channelling resources that are already there and helping the education process on the Hill.
Tobacco kills more people than drug addiction to heroin, cocaine, or marijuana or than motor vehicle accidents. In the United States, every year, tobacco kills more people than those afflictions. It is interesting to note the amount of money and initiative spent for law enforcement in those areas and yet we pay minor lip service to attempting to prevent health damage due to tobacco. It is absolutely critical that we do that. On this Hill, the example could start.
I commend the Minister of National Health and Welfare for statements that he has made. Those statements must be translated into action. They are not strong enough. Remember that smokers want to quit, but they are in the grip of a powerful addiction, a powerful drug, promoted by tobacco companies, absolutely unscrupulous companies, which are targeting children and Third World countries and attempting to push this product. What we have is the Government of Canada making statements that it recognizes the problem but failing to act or failing to act strongly enough.
First, there must be an absolute ban on importing tobacco products into Canada. The health of the population of this country is at stake. We would not permit cocaine to come into Canada and yet it does less damage. We would not permit heroin or crack to come into this country. We put enormous law enforcement against those drugs, but we permit tobacco products to come in and kill far more than any of those products.
There must be an absolute ban on any kind of tobacco advertising and promotion by tobacco companies of events in this country. A stroke of the pen does that. It begins to erode and break the tobacco companies'

market. It is an absolute must. The carrot and the stick, prohibit it.
There is no reason why we should assist smokers to gain the product. Increase the tax on tobacco-pick a figure-100 per cent a year for 10 years. By the end of 10 years, it would certainly be very difficult to smoke. There would be a powerful incentive to get involved in a quit-smoking program. The more incentives that we can provide, the more people will quit, the more healthy this population will be, in terms of the individual smokers as well as the people affected by the health hazards of secondary smoke.
Incidentally, it is projected that 330 people a year die of cancers and health problems related to secondary smoke such as spouses and children of smokers who are affected by this. We cannot tolerate it; we must prohibit it. We must prohibit the import, tax tobacco products and absolutely prohibit any tobacco advertising and promoting.
The next thing is that the Third World is being targeted to take up the slack where there is market erosion. Market expansion and profit expansion of the tobacco companies is going on and it is by exporting to Third World countries. A ban on the export of the product would fix it at least from Canadians. There should be an initiative through the World Health Organization and the United Nations to stop other countries from doing it. These are the things the government could be doing nationally on the prohibition side to create a healthier Canadian population, to prevent the death that goes on as a result of tobacco smoking, the selling of a drug that is killing Canadians. We could see that happen if the government took this seriously. I know the minister of health takes it seriously. I know the Liberal Party takes it seriously and certainly we take it seriously.
There is also the health promotion side of it, the carrot and the stick. We have no truck or trade with the tobacco companies. They are selling a drug. They are the purveyors of death. That is absolutely certain.
They are targeting our children, our teenagers in those schools. They are talking about selling smaller packs of cigarettes, selling packs of cigarettes with sunglasses in them, or CD disks in order to niche market this stuff to our kids. We have to stop it. It is absolutely ludicrous. We

October 29, 1990

have to set the example, as members of Parliament and people who work in this institution, to other Canadians and to our own children that this has got to stop.
On the promotion side of it, we have a health unit on this Hill with dedicated people who staff it, who have offered quit-smoking programs on this Hill, but they do not seem to have the budget or the support of members of Parliament, of the Speaker, and of the human resources directorate. We should be putting a quit-smoking program in place. There should be a careful survey of smokers on Parliament Hill. There should be a highly advertised program to attract people into that with incentives: time off work to participate, not on a Friday night or a weekend or after work when everybody is tired and it is difficult to avoid your other commitments, but let us give an incentive where those people are paid to take that program.
Our benefit is simply a healthier population that has proven more productive. There are fewer days of illness for non-smokers than smokers. The workforce on this Hill would be more productive. The workforce on this Hill and the people who live and work here would be healthier. The return to health care budgets, to productivity, would offset the costs of providing a quit-smoking program.
Then we need some resources to follow up. Not everybody can shake this drug the first time around. If there is follow-up and continuing incentive and support to do it, we could be of tremendous assistance to stopping the smoking on this Hill. Nobody is attempting to remove the rights of smokers, to belittle them, badger them. It is simply too important a health care item.
It is the voluntary destruction of a person's health and the committing of our health care resources to treating them when those injuries occur, for the loss of productivity in common tasks that we all share here, that is preventable. We are all the beneficiaries of that. We must move on it, Mr. Speaker, and we must be strong.
In terms of the taxation item, if there was an enormous effort to tax the industry and to prevent the development of this industry in Canada, we would have to look seriously at conversion. There is no reason that tobacco farmers should be totally and economically hung out to dry. There should be a move in this country to reduce
production by 10 per cent a year to the year 2000, when we are out of the business totally.
The taxes raised could assist farmers to move into different operations. The incentive again is to provide grants or forgivable loans to individuals who convert from tobacco to another product. We could attack this from the bottom of the industry, where tobacco is grown and processed, to the very front end of it where our children are standing out in front of the elementary schools, the junior secondary schools, and the senior secondary schools initiating themselves into a habit that is going to kill quite a number of them.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of people who wish to speak on this issue this afternoon. It is my hope that your office will rule on the question of privilege of the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants that this institution must not permit smoking within the confines of the House of Commons, the Chamber, or its opposition lobbies.
The Speaker's office should take the initiative to stop smoking in members' offices. How can we turn around to our employees and say: "There is a penalty for you smoking on this Hill," and yet at the same time permit it elsewhere. That example has got to happen, Mr. Speaker.
Let us get into our health unit and order the director general of the human resources branch to get a clear statement of goals and objectives, to get a powerful stop-smoking program on this Hill and with the incentives to make it successful in the follow-up.
The last statement is an appeal to the minister of health. Good so far, but statements are not enough. We need a powerful attempt to stop this industry in its tracks and save Canadian lives that are going to be lost, and lives of our children that are going to be lost.

subtopic: PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the member for North Island-Powell River for reminding us once again of the considerable importance and significant act that was taken by this Parliament not very long ago in its previous session. I think I am right in reminding him that it was one of his colleagues, the former member for Broadview-Greenwood, Lynn McDonald, who initiated this very important step that was made here in the previous Parliament.
October 29, 1990

Bill C-27, the Non-Smokers' Health Act received Royal Assent on July 29, 1989, along with the regulations made pursuant to the act, and came into force on December 29, 1989.
Members will recall that that bill was given all-party approval. It also received extensive support from health organizations, employer and employee groups, consumer organizations, anti-smoking groups and the public at large.
Essentially, the act prohibits smoking in the workplaces under federal jurisdiction except in designated smoking rooms or areas. Perhaps to the degree that the member for North Island-Powell River is able to point out that we have not sufficiently eliminated smoking in either members' offices or in other parts of this building, it may be partly attributable to the fact that I am not aware if we have made available any alternatives for those who on their own private decision have continued to smoke. Certainly in the winter and other times of the year we see people outside of these buildings and other public buildings puffing furiously. This may not be the most humane or even sensible way to proceed.
There is no doubt, however, that research has demonstrated that breathing second-hand tobacco smoke contributes to, or causes a variety of health problems. Now that we have eliminated in the first instance the public acceptability of smoking in public buildings, there is this problem for those who are very much affected by second-hand smoke.
Tobacco smoke contains in excess of 4,000 different chemicals. Some of them are highly toxic, and 43 at least are known to be cancer-causing substances. Studies show that second-hand tobacco smoke worsen systems of pre-existing conditions, such as angina, emphysema, acute respiratory diseases, asthma, hay fever and other allergies. Prolonged exposure may also increases instances of lung cancer and heart disease.
A recent report examined the effects of second-hand tobacco smoke and makes reference to the United States Surgeon-General's conclusion that involuntary smoking can cause lung cancer. Children of parents who smoke face increased risks of respiratory disease. The separation of smokers from non-smokers in the same air space may reduce, but does not entirely eliminate exposure to environmental tobacco smoke for non-smokers.
Private Members' Business
A recent study by the Environmental Protection Agency in the United States states that if you add up all the lung cancer deaths from other cancer risks which the EPA regulates, the total number of deaths from all those sources would be less than the number of deaths now attributed to environmental tobacco smoke in an indoor environment.
The purpose of the act, therefore, is to protect both employees and the public who have access to the workplace from the adverse effects of such exposure. Under the act, employers under federal jurisdiction have a responsibility to ensure that persons do not smoke, except in designated smoking rooms or smoking areas. If an employee contravenes the act, the employer is expected after due warning to take disciplinary measures against that employee, consistent with standard employer-employee disciplinary practices. In large measure, however, the act is self-regulating, although there are more stringent enforcement measures available in cases of flagrant contradictions.
The act has been in effect for some 10 months and I believe that it has been received in the workplace with remarkable equanimity. My friend for North Island-Powell River mentions that there are still 20 per cent of the offices where there is the obvious evidence of those who are still smoking.
An equally remarkable statistic is the fact that 80 per cent of the offices do not now reflect that. When one thinks about the heavy incidents of smoking, politics and smoke-filled back rooms, I think in the course of less than a year it has been a remarkable, most impressive change, one that is very significant. I want to say a word about that in a moment.
Attitudes toward smoking have changed rapidly and profoundly. The right of workers to a healthy smoke-free environment is no longer a matter of debate. When we think about environmental issues generally and matters of personal health and safety specifically, we have to say that in terms of what has happened in the Parliament Buildings over the last year or two nothing is more impressive, in my estimation, than the very real change of atmosphere-no pun intended-with respect to the way in which smoking, if not entirely eliminated, has been reduced so substantially as to be truly significant.

October 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
Over the course of the last year you will recall that collaborating with you, Sir, and with members of the environment committee-and I would like to pay tribute to both, including my seatmate from Parry Sound-Mus-koka and others-we have been attempting to make the Parliament Buildings and environs a model of environmental responsibility.
Another example which I think is quite impressive is that of styrofoam cups, which have been used in abundance here for years. We were up to close to one million styrofoam cups per year. In the course of making the transition away from styrofoam in the last year, we have eliminated by half a million the number of styrofoam cups presently being used.
Major changes in lifestyle and personal practices can take place when there is a will to do so. With respect to smoking, we have already been impressed by the changes that have taken place. I would like to emphasize that the Non-Smokers' Health Act applies to all workplaces under federal jurisdiction, including the House of Commons and the Senate. Section 2 of the act is explicit on that point. Members of Parliament and their support staff are subject to the same requirements as the rest of those under federal jurisdiction. We have ensured that we have not imposed on others legislation with which we ourselves are not prepared to comply.
It is true, as the hon. member for North Island-Powell River has suggested, that there is still 20 per cent of the offices where there are some incidents of smoking. I would like to commend the other 80 per cent, that other four-fifths that have made this very real change in lifestyle and practice in their own offices and environs.
There are still going to be complaints-and I believe we should be aware of them and take appropriate responsibility-about members who are smoking in restricted areas such as their own offices. We simply cannot allow this to continue indefinitely. I certainly strongly recommend to you, Mr. Speaker, that all members of Parliament and their support staff take upon themselves to comply with the regulations in the Non-Smokers' Health Act and thereby set an important example for all the very real and important reasons suggested by the hon. member for North Island-Powell River and certainly well known to all members of this House.

subtopic: PARLIAMENT HILL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, cigarette smoke adversely affects smokers and nonsmokers alike. It harms adults and children as well as the unborn in the wombs of their mothers. Yes, smoking is a serious hazard to health.
I therefore rise today to speak on this particular motion from our colleague from North Island-Powell River to reinforce the concern I and other Canadians have and should have about this deadly poison: smoking.
I am confident that all members of this House will agree that smoking is a health hazard. Since the hon. member proposed his motion on June 27, 1989, we have seen improvement in the House, as noted, from the House of Commons smoking policy dated November 1989. We have seen improvement, but we would like to reinforce the idea of the danger of smoking.
Smoking related diseases kill some 35,000 Canadians every year. Second-hand smoke causes about 350 deaths each year in Canada. Deaths due to smoking are not due only to cancer that victims develop. No doubt smoke is a class a carcinogen in the ranks of asbestos and benzene. However, deaths from smoking also occur from other chronic debilitating lung diseases such as emphysema, chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis-diseases that make it difficult for patients to breathe freely. This disease not only kills but also incapacitates a large number of Canadians.
This issue is not getting the prompt attention necessary to make this disease disappear from Canada. Regulations governing labelling of cigarette packages have again been delayed by this government. We have seen that. It appears the tobacco lobby is allowed to win some battles. We cannot afford to be complacent. We cannot afford to sit down. Seeing the dangers of smoke, we have to remain vigilant.
Ten years or so ago the idea of banning smoking on the job would have appeared outrageous to most Canadians. Today we should be outraged that smoking is still allowed. The challenge is clear. Ten years from now we should be able to say and wonder why smoking started in the first place in the history of mankind and continued to be condoned and abetted by governments. I do not want to wait until the turn of the century for cessation of smoking to happen. Smoking is killing our adults, is
October 29, 1990

killing our growing children, and is even killing the unborn.
The House of Commons should set the example for the rest of the country and completely ban smoking to the extent that no one is allowed to smoke on the grounds of Parliament Hill, let alone on the doorsteps. I am promoting today that smoking be prohibited everywhere and anywhere on government property. We have an obligation to set the model. We should be a paragon to others.
Those who do smoke, we must understand them as well. We must provide them with the means and the necessary resources for them to quit the habit with ease. According to senior scientists at the Addiction Research Foundation in Toronto, those who try to quit the smoking habit face three difficult hurdles: nicotine addiction, psychological habituation, and emotional reaction. Each smoker is a separate clinical case. Any smoking cessation program, therefore, should be tailor made to the individual. I congratulate the leadership of the House of Commons for allowing an assistance program to be available to smokers who want to stop smoking, but we must see to it that everyone is making use of this program.
Commercial gimmicks should not replace proven effective methods. For the method to be successful we should have policies in place so as to include the necessity of providing psychological and financial help to those who want to quit smoking. As along as a person wants to quit the habit, the federal government should be there to provide all the necessary assistance.
In the interim, designated places must be available for those who cannot yet break the habit. Designated spaces ought to be adequately ventilated. As well, the employees of the tobacco industry must be helped to find alternative types of work. If we do this then we are serious in our purpose. We realize that smoking is so harmful that even if only the cost of health care is taken into account in our country, there is a big price to pay, not to mention loss of human lives.
One approach that has been proven effective to further counteract smoking, particularly among the young, is to increase taxes on smoking. We should do that. We should tax smoking to death, if need be, but we must remember that that is only one step. We must link
Private Members' Business
health care policy and tax policy together if we are to stop this bad habit in the country.
I am very pleased to speak to this motion. I salute my colleague for bringing it forth for further consideration. If we have the will we can always find the way.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to address the House on the evolution of the Non-Smokers' Health Act and how it was developed to ensure that the health of visitors and employees of Parliament Hill would be protected.
The legislation which eventually became the NonSmokers' Health Act was introduced in the House of Commons as Bill C-204, which became the act. It was supported on both sides of the House and Senate, as well as by various groups representing labour, health organizations, consumers, employers, citizens, anti-smoking groups, et cetera, and given Royal Assent in June 1988.
By Order in Council in December 1988, certain ministers were made responsible for the implementation and administration of the act. I take exception to the hon. member for North Island-Powell River suggesting that we have not been leading in this initiative. It is really misrepresenting this government's actions to the people of Canada.
I want to point out a couple of areas that I am sure the hon. member would applaud if he were to stop and think about them. For example, when the Minister of Transport, who is one of the designated ministers I talked about earlier, took the case of the new legislation, Bill C-204, to the common carriers, the carriers of Canada immediately followed the regulations, including Air Ontario based in London, Ontario, and brought in non-smoking flights. This applied to flights to international destinations as well.
The member would certainly join with me in congratulating Air Canada which is a way out in front in this particular endeavour by having no smoking at all on its flights in the future.
Clearly the act which became law under this government was passed on to Canadians who picked it up and are moving ahead with gusto.
Last June this Parliament had the opportunity to host 300 of our colleagues from 30 countries in the Council of Europe sponsored environment conference here in Ot-

October 29, 1990
Private Members' Business
tawa. We brought in this law, Bill C-204 with all its regulations, into effect, so the Europeans learned firsthand from Canadian parliamentarians that possibly they could take some of these regulations and these ideas for legislation home to their own countries and bring nonsmokers' rights to the attention of their own legislatures.
There has been clear leadership both within this Etouse as well as within this government. I think the member for North Island-Powell River could reflect on that and say: yes, this government has been active and has been very supportive of the health of Canadians in wanting to do everything about it.
That is not to say that there have not been problems. In its original form, the act contains certain deficiencies that would have made it difficult to administer and apply. For example, it lacked a system of inspection and enforcement and had as well technical and drafting problems.
For example, section 3 of the act required that every employer provide a smoke-free environment in which all employees could perform the duties that are directly or indirectly related to their employment. This requirement would have made it necessary for concentrations of tobacco smoke to be measured, which technically and administratively is not feasible with any degree of accuracy.
There was also confusion about the terms smoking room and smoking area, as well as the definition of employer. Clearly there were things to overcome, but again our government has not been negligent and has worked on these. Without departing from the spirit and intent of the act, amendments were sought to provide a system of inspection and enforcement, to correct its deficiencies and to enhance its workability.
Bill C-27, an act to amend the Non-Smokers' Health Act, was passed by the House of Commons on June 26, 1989. It is very clear that this government has not fumbled the ball. It has stayed on top of this issue because it knows that it is important to Canadians. It knows that the health of Canadians is first and foremost on their minds, as any good government would. In fact, policies and regulations must be in effect that will help Canadians as we move forward to be the champions of the 21st century. It is evident that we already have
legislation designed to prevent smoking on Parliament Hill except in designated rooms. It should be emphasized that such rooms cannot be members' offices.
The employer is responsible for enforcing the Nonsmokers' Health Act in the workplace. If workers do not abide by the rules in the act, the employer is supposed to take appropriate action. Such action would first involve a warning to the employee who violates the act. If this type of response proves to be unsuccessful in achieving the employee's compliance with the act, further action with respect to that worker would have to be taken by the employer. This action should be consistent with traditional disciplinary procedures established by the employer in consultation with employees.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that goes without saying, it is common sense. The fact that Canadians are grasping this act of the Government of Canada, Bill C-204, shows that they know that its time has come, that the health of Canadians is at stake. Canadians have risen to that challenge both nationally through their actions, the fact that they do not ask government to give them no-smoking campaigns, and they do not ask the government to pay for them to stop being smokers. They know the responsibility is theirs. They are readily coming forward, accepting this responsibility to their fellow Canadians and acting appropriately.
This message has not got lost on our colleagues that we share this world with. The fact that other parliamentarians as they leave this House see how far we have come on such health measures as this one, are now going back to their legislatures around the world seriously looking at what Canada, what this Progressive Conservative government has done for Canadians and saying these people know the way, they are the future. It is a pleasure to speak on this today.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to comment briefly on Motion M-510 which was introduced by the hon. member for North Island-Powell River and which reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should demonstrate to Canadians that Members of Parliament and their support staff are subject to the same regulations enforced in Federal buildings with regard to the smoking of tobacco products by banning immediately all smoking of tobacco products on Parliament Hill.
October 29, 1990

I listened very closely to all my colleagues who spoke on this issue.

I do agree with him totally that smoking is not good for one's health, whether one smokes or someone is smoking next to one. I think it has been proven. Everyone understands that. Practically everyone seems to accept this.
I think the approach is one of a totalitarian state. We give people authority sometimes but they are just a group of do-gooders wanting to protect the health of everyone, including their own. Of course, we have to be careful.
I am a non-smoker. I have never smoked any time during my life except for once when I was 14 years old. I tried a cigarette and I was so sick that never, never again did I ever touch one. I got the feeling that I was absolutely allergic to it. However, I understand that some people are not allergic to smoking like I am, but my allergy does not make me Attila the Hun where I command and order everyone to do as I feel is best for them.
That is the part that I really find disgusting in this approach. We should have programs.

-programs which encourage people not to smoke, programs which encourage people to quit smoking, programs to ban advertising to promote smoking. Smokers have various options, mainly cigarettes, cigars, and pipes. I am sure my colleagues all agree that we used to have a generation of cigar smokers-practically extinct by now, thank God!-a practice that was absolutely disgracious. It was enough to make you choke and, besides, it stank!
There were people who smoked a pipe and some still do. Some people don't mind the smell at all, in fact they enjoy it.
As far as cigarette smoking is concerned, the smell is far less offensive. In the case of cigarettes, we see people who have been inveterate smokers for many years. For some people it is pretty hard, and in some cases almost impossible, to shake the habit and quit smoking. I know
Private Members' Business
members of this House, employees, friends of the family and even family members who smoke.
I think the key word is moderation. First of all, people should be encouraged not to smoke. However, we should not go overboard with our regulations. We must not be stricter than our own rules. When we go past public buildings, whether they are federal, provincial, municipal or regional, where the rule is: No smoking, it is a common sight to see employees, winter and summer, come out of these buildings and pollute the space outside the building, and I am referring to visual pollution. There is also pollution in the real sense, when they drop their cigarette stubs all over the place, because the people who run the buildings close their eyes to the problem and refuse to co-operate and accommodate inveterate smokers by providing ash receptacles to keep the place clean. I think it is ridiculous that enforcing these rules means people have to go outside to smoke in the middle of winter. I wonder how much sick leave is taken as a result of the fact that people are forced to go outside to smoke for ten minutes, without a coat on, and then go back to their jobs.
I think it is unfair that people who are addicted to smoking don't have a place where they are allowed to smoke. I think the Minister of Transport's decision to prevent smoking on board aircraft is ridiculous if it applies to all flights and all aircraft. There should be a space for people who are addicted to smoking and who have to smoke.
I repeat, I hate the smell of smoke, and I can't stand people smoking in front of me. However, what I find even more distressing is the authoritarian attitude of certain people-

CRUISE MISSILE TESTING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in January, 1988, the Canadian government said it would continue to test Cruise missiles until progress was made on disarmament.
It is now 1990 and we have seen a major change in east-west relations with detente, co-operation, and arms reductions. Yet, today, another U.S. Cruise missile will be tested in northern Canada.
We are now in the post cold war era, with a treaty on intermediate nuclear weapons already signed and treaties on conventional arms, chemical weapons, and strategic missiles well advanced. What then is the purpose of continued testing of U.S. Cruise missiles in Canada?
Nuclear weapons are still one of the greatest threats to human existence. On October 15, the Soviet Union reaffirmed its readiness to become a non-nuclear state, if other nuclear countries did the same. Canada should support that goal and put an immediate end to Cruise missile testing in Canada.

SCHIZOPHRENIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one out of every 100 Canadians is affected by schizophrenia.
This disease uses 7 per cent of all hospital beds and is responsible for almost $2 billion in hospital expenses each year. Yet the federal government's contribution to research for this serious mental disorder is only $2 million.
Schizophrenia is a disease about which we know veiy little. We have some ideas about what causes it and how it can be treated, but we are nowhere near an understanding of this serious mental disorder. The amount of federal expenditure on research is out of line with the seriousness and the economic and social impact of this disease in Canadian society.
I would encourage the government to provide more funds for research to reduce health care costs and to improve the lot of those affected with schizophrenia.

WOOD BUFFALO NATIONAL PARK
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 3,200 bison in Wood Buffalo National Park are the only remain'ng free-roaming herd in the world.
Last February, I stated in the House that the government would be making the largest wildlife management
mistake in the history of the country if it proceeded with the eradication of the Wood Buffalo herd. When the environmental panel recommended total slaughter in August, I immediately wrote to the Deputy Prime Minister and asked him to reconsider the options.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: GASOLINE PRICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is a problem in the way gas retailers are setting their pump prices. The pump price is a reflection of upstream production costs. Consumers are aware that costs must be covered and they accept this.
What they have a hard time accepting is the method of pricing which delays the increase in the pump price until the supply has made its way through the production chain. This problem is emphasized by the rising pump prices seen throughout the lower mainland and in my riding of Fraser Valley East, while crude prices have dropped significantly. Valley drivers now pay the same as Vancouver, even though Vancouver has an additional transportation tax.
The existence of low crude prices and high pump prices is incongruous and assaults the sensibilities of the consumer. Pump pricing that reflects the price of crude is a more appropriate system. Perhaps the first in, last out method of supply pricing should be changed to last in, first out. This would prevent any misperception of gouging and ensure a measure of congruity between the wellhead and the pump price.
The industry needs to take a serious look at pricing policy. In the valley, 69.9 cents a litre is out of sync with the rest of Canada and far too high.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Justice and concerns the Great Whale project at James Bay. The project's infrastructure includes an airport, a road that crosses territory where Crees have rights, and a road that crosses navigable waters.

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
subtopic: GREAT WHALE PROJECT
speechtext:

There has been no decision by Quebec at this point to begin any work or commission any work, without an environmental review.
Certainly it is not the intention of the federal government to grant any kind of a licence or to allow any kind of work to proceed, that is associated with that project, without the federal review.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary is directed to the Prime Minister. Why does this government refuse to make a clear stand on this issue? The federal government cannot deny it has jurisdiction over airports. The federal government cannot deny it has jurisdiction over navigable waters, and the federal government cannot deny it has jurisdiction over wildlife. Does the government intend to follow its own guidelines? Does the Prime Minister intend to settle immediately the present debate in Quebec on infrastructure? Does the government intend to show the kind of leadership it has failed to show so far in other environmental cases in Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Forestry
subtopic: GREAT WHALE PROJECT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps my language is not clear enough, but certainly the minister has spoken on this issue several times.
The message could not be clearer. There will be an environmental review process.
The minister happens to be in Montreal today on urgent business, and he asked me to respond to questions like this one as they come forth.
There has not been the commissioning of any work of any sort. There cannot be any clearer statement than the one that has been made. Ideally the EARP process should be conducted in partnership with the province of Quebec. Failing that, there will be a full environmental review process carried out, as other Canadians and the people in Quebec would expect us to do, including any works that are associated with the dam project, infrastructures such as airport roads, and any other work.

Dioxins are ubiquitous in the environment. Much food in Canada has trace elements of dioxin in it, without posing any threat to human health. The difficulty is that it is possible to discover very, very, small, minute quantities of this. speechtext:
The House resumed from Tuesday, October 23, consideration of the motion of Mr. McDermid that Bill C-84, an act respecting the privatization of the national petroleum company of Canada, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee; and the amendment of Mr. Lee:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the word "That" and substituting the following therefor:
"this House oppose in principle Bill C-84, An Act respecting the privatization of the National Petroleum Company of Canada, because it considers it irresponsible to abandon public sector involvement in the Canadian petroleum industry in the absence of a coherent Canadian federal government energy policy at a time of increasing international uncertainty with regard to petroleum supply."

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted, quite appropriately, at the end of our session the other day, I had just finished recounting some of the history of Petro-Canada.
As you know, Petro-Canada now has a history of some 15 years of operation behind it. Its current situation and prospects are conditioned, to a significant extent, by that past history. Understandably, some of the high-risk frontier investments which it undertook in the early stages of its existence, in fulfilment of its energy policy role, have not yet produced commercial revenues. As a result, Petro-Canada's financial performance is now not as robust as in the case of some of its privately-owned competitors. Despite this, under the new direction that it has had, the company has become a major player on the Canadian oil and gas scene and it is now ready to face reality by placing its shares in the free market.
Petro-Canada is now a major, integrated company and it is the largest Canadian-controlled company, with the second largest proven reserves of oil and natural gas liquids and the fourth largest natural gas reserves of any company in Canada. It has the second largest refining capacity and gasoline sales in Canada, and it has established major holdings in Canada, in existing and future energy megaprojects. Petro-Canada will be a major force in the Canadian oil and gas industry far into the future. It is time for it to cut the apron strings, to stop relying on the public purse and to get on with its business in a truly competitive environment.
The reasons for my support of Petro-Canada's privatization are simple and clear. State ownership of Petro-Canada is not necessary for the government to achieve public policies' objectives. Petro-Canada needs capital to develop to its full potential and it is much better to raise capital voluntarily, through a share issue, than it is to further burden the Canadian taxpayer with debt and higher taxes to pay that debt back. When Petro-Canada was created in the 1970s, we were told by the then Liberal government that a centrally planned, state owned oil company was needed to achieve three national objectives.
First, the company was to be the great oil finder. It would increase oil and gas supplies in Canada by exploring for new sources, especially in the frontier areas off Canada's coasts and in the Arctic. Mr. Speaker, I doubt that one barrel of new oil has been discovered by Petro-Canada that the oil industry would not have discovered on its own. Second, the company was to be a window on the industry to help governments see through the corporate veil of secrecy so that it could formulate national energy policies. Policies such as the National Energy Program were a total disaster, certainly for Alberta, and in my opinion, for the whole of Canada.
Third, the company was to be a negotiator that would somehow arrange special nation-to-nation deals that would guarantee oil supplies. I have already explained what a flop that was.
In the 1990s it is clear, if it was not always clear, that state ownership of a national oil company is no longer needed to achieve such public policy objectives. The government has access to the information it requires through agencies such as the Petroleum Monitoring Agency, the Canadian Oil and Gas Lands Administra-
October 29, 1990

tion and the National Energy Board. There are many other ways for the government to ensure energy supplies through state-to-state negotiations, should they be required.
In short, there are no valid reasons for state ownership of Pelro-Canada. History will decide if there ever were any, other than the desire of central Canadian Liberals to put a stranglehold on western Canada. It is a time to put things right, time for Petro-Canada to step out of the shadows and subject itself to the full light of public and investor scrutiny.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will be very brief in my comment. I will present a question to my colleague as well.
The present chief executive officer of PetroCan suggested not three or four months ago that if the timing was not right to go ahead with the privatization of PetroCan that it would not proceed. May I suggest that the timing could not be worse. If this is not a bad time, I wonder what the chief executive officer would describe as a bad time.
I do not want to get into the prices and the pitfalls of what we are proceeding with, but I would like him to comment on that.
Going from the financial angle to the human side of things, I am told by PetroCan dealers, not only in my community but in other communities, that in some of the bigger communities the PetroCan people were told not to comment on the privatization of this PetroCan oil company that is owned by Canadians. The people in my community were told nothing at all. Is there not something wrong with that? With regard to the livelihood of these people and the future of their families, should they not have been kept abreast as to what was going to happen or what was happening to them, rather than reading it in the newspapers just like the rest of us?

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the comments and questions from my hon. friend from Sault Ste. Marie.
With regard to the timing, I am sure that there is never a time when he would say that it is the right time. He and his party have always wanted to have our industry, not only the oil industry, but other industries, centrally planned and controlled so that there is no ability for the public to participate directly and to be entrepreneurial in their activities. This is his philosophy. As far as that is
Government Orders
concerned, it is a very difficult question for me to answer to his satisfaction.
However, as far as I am concerned at the present time there exists a situation where it is clear that Petro-Canada should be stepping out. There is no logic to having a company which controls only 6 per cent of the upstream resource finding in Canada, and 18 per cent of the marketplace, to be trying to use that position to leverage itself into a public policy position. There are much better levers that a government can use if it wants to, and in fact I would say that I hope it does not use them.
As far as the human considerations are concerned regarding the communications within Petro-Canada, I have not been personally involved in those; but knowing how major oil companies work I am sure, insofar as it has been possible, that communication has been quite full and complete within the company.
To say that there is no communication and that people do not know what has been going on is totally inappropriate because the government's plan has been well forecast and stated. I think anyone working in the company would celebrate the fact that the company is now going to expand its asset base and be able to perform more effectively in the marketplace and therefore they will have securer jobs.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask the member a question in an attempt to resolve what I think is possibly a dichotomy; at least it certainly confuses me.
As the member and his party as the government recommend to all Canadians that the government abandon oil and gas exploration activity, abandon the vertically integrated oil company approach to participation in the marketplace and in fact abandon the whole field to the marketplace, I am curious why at the same time the government has rushed full force into the Hibernia oil development with billions of dollars in subsidies and has done it hand in hand with Petro-Canada, which maintains a 25 interest in the Hibernia oil development.
Could the member explain the difference of philosophy there? I do not understand how the government can send the whole business of oil and gas and energy policy back to the private sector on one hand and can put so many resources on its own into the Hibernia oil development, which has definitely been defined as not being a

October 29, 1990
Government Orders
marketplace venture. It would not exist if it were simply market forces.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to answer that question because quite frankly it is one that I am asked quite often in Alberta.
The situation is this: we cannot compare what is going on, for example, in the western oil and gas industry with what is going on in Hibernia. The Newfoundland oil and gas industry is back where the western oil and gas industry was about 30 years ago. That industry needs support for its basic infrastructure.
We have a situation where the proponents of the project are being asked in effect to build a company, to build one piece of equipment and then effectively close that factory down. To do that they are obviously going to need a subsidy. Of course we are quite sure that that factory will be there to build future units on an ongoing basis, but in order to get it started there has to be a subsidy. This is a very fair situation.
We are not providing equity investment, and I think that is very important, because we are not getting the government involved in equity participation. We have the government providing the basic subsidy and loan guarantees. This is fundamentally sound for the oil and gas industry in Newfoundland in the stage that it is at at the present time.
This is not at all different to the type of support that was given, for example, to the oil sands projects in the early days of Alberta's history where they were given special tax breaks, special royalty breaks and so on to get the industry started.
It is a very fundamental and fair comparison, one that I fully support. We are not getting the government involved through Hibernia in equity participation in the oil and gas industry.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after listening to my hon. colleague opposite, I am wondering why the government does not use such a reasonable voice, in a more positive light, in some of the deliberations that it has. I find his presentation convincing, but I do not know if I am completely persuaded. I was tempted to ask him a question, but I did not want in any way to indicate that I was mischievous in the kind of
question I would pose. He is obviously on his own in the positions that he has taken. He has pointed out some very good and solid reasons why Petro-Canada should exist. He has pointed out its success.
I might say that that success was underscored and emphasized by the head of Petro-Canada, Bill Hopper, on Morningside on October 27, 1990. When he was asked about whether Petro-Canada had been good for its consumers, his response-and I think I quote him accurately-was: "The purpose it served was to go out aggressively and do a lot of exploration in the frontier. That is its first purpose. It spent a lot of money, brought a lot of people with us, but we also found how Hibernia, Terra Nova, heavy oils and tar sands all have been good for Canadian oil supply."
It is fair to say that a private company could not have been as aggressive in the frontier as we have. Our purpose at the time was not to have a bottom line profit, but to find carbon resources for Canada. It did that job very well. I notice that my colleague opposite, in his presentation a few moments ago, pointed out that it had been most successful in the exploration field.
He suggested that perhaps a private sector company might have been equally successful or that the oil might have been found-and I stress the words "might have been found"-by other corporations as well. The point of the matter that it has been found under the auspices of Petro-Canada.
Even the minister who is so keen to privatize it, as reported in Hansard on October 10, gave his presentation as to why there should be privatization. He said:
Clearly Petro-Canada has established itself as a major integrated energy producer in Canada-Tbday it represents 6 per cent of the exploration and development side of the industry and 19 per cent of the refining and marketing business in Canada.
With that kind of success, one has to ask oneself why we have to privatize. I think there is a larger question which quite frankly is about why the government refuses to use Petro-Canada as an instrument of public policy. That is really what is underlying this debate.
I think that is the reason why the minister opposite, who is following this debate diligently, after only two hours and fifteen minutes of debate-and, Mr. Speaker, if you check Hansard you will see that we are not off at
October 29, 1990

all-stood on a point of order and asked that we apply time allocation to this bill.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: I gave notice that I would be.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That is right. He really wanted to give notice that he was going to do it on the very next occasion that he had because it was ruled out of order by the Speaker. He went ahead and moved a motion. The point that all hon. members ask themselves is why he would want to do that so quickly if what he was talking about was privatization, or whether he was in fact afraid of the issue of using Petro-Canada as an instrument of public policy. He knows full well that all he has to do is check our public accounts. Since 1984 the government has not spent one penny on Petro-Canada. There have been no government funds into Petro-Canada. Notwithstanding, the company has been very successful.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Because you wouldn't give us an agreement.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I only quoted what he said in Hansard. If he wants to retract what he said in Hansard, I am willing to give up my spot right now and have him retract everything. While he is at it, he might even go ahead and retract his bill.
He would do everybody a favour. It did not take long. Two hours and fifteen minutes is about as much time as it took for him to stand.
My esteemed colleague from Scarborough-Rouge River stood and gave a very succinct, very incisive and very thorough analysis of what was wrong with this bill. The minister opposite was shame faced and red faced when this happened. I am not referring to the fact that he was beginning to acquire a different political colour, but it is one that happens when someone is embarrassed.
I have to give credit where credit is due. My NDP colleague from a riding in Winnipeg continued in the same vein as started by my colleague from Scarborough-Rouge River and just reamed of this bill. It is poorly drawn. It is wrong. Its economic bases and financial presumptions are all distorted.
The fourth speaker was a member of the government side. Within a couple of minutes the minister decided that this was time to ask for time allocation. He wanted to show that we were going to stop this debate as quickly as possible. What these colleagues of ours were showing
Government Orders
is that Petro-Canada had not been a drain on our debt nor on our deficit.
The government has been careful over the course of the last several months to talk about how to reduce the deficit. Everything is deficit reduction driven and nothing else. What happens is the minister who acknowledges that there are no government funds going to Petro-Canada says: "No, no. We have to privatize this thing".
They will start with a 15 per cent sale offering right off the bat. That sale, given the facts that are incontestable right now, will obviously bring only marginal benefit to the government deficit reduction, if any at all. In fact on that 15 per cent, the highest estimate of what it is supposed to raise is somewhere around $700 million, according to today's prices and today's values on the marketplace. That $700 million is not going toward deficit reduction; it is going back into the company. It is a great deal.
My colleague from London is looking at making a few investments. He is wondering whether this would be a good place for Canadians to go. You go ahead and buy a 15 per cent share in the company. Then you get the money back, so you automatically get a 15 per cent saving or a reduction on your investment.
This is good finances on the part of the government. There is no net benefit to the government in terms of debt reduction or deficit reduction.
What are they doing? The company is profitable. Just the other day in the House we had reference again to the financial statements of Petro-Canada, which in the first three quarters indicated net revenues after expenditures of $84 million. It is not losing money.
All hon. colleagues have their calculators out. They are going to say: "If we divide this $84 million in the first three quarters by three and multiply by four, we discover that we have about $102 million in net revenues after expenditures for 1990". That is not bad. That is a good profit. If that $100 million were to carry a loan at 15 per cent, it would probably generate another loan of $680 million.
The government says it needs somewhere around $500 million to $700 million. It has an opportunity. It can cariy it on the basis of the profits it will make on this company; but the government says: "No, no, no. We have an

October 29, 1990
Government Orders
opportunity to raise funds differently. We don't have to borrow. What we do is sell off part of the company".
Rather than think in terms of having a government contribution, if we go a bit farther down the road we see that we cannot become too heavily indebted. The debt to asset ratio for Petro-Canada is 1.9 per cent to 8.6 per cent, so roughly 22 per cent of all of its assets are encumbered. Essentially we are talking of a very low encumbrance level for a company.
If it is true that the borrowing is tough, then when we take a look at the debt to asset ratio and at the revenues after expenditures and ask ourselves-and all Canadians have been asking themselves this with respect to privatization of Petro-Canada-why it is that one of our profitable companies, a Canadian company in which we have invested billions of dollars, a company that is doing well on the marketplace, a company that the minister stands up and says is a very productive, very profitable and very efficient company, is going to be sold off, the first offering for 15 per cent.
For those of us who are also concerned about jobs and where the government's priorities are, it is important to keep in mind that Petro-Canada employs some 8,753 employees. If we take a look at what has happened in the past with other companies that have been privatized and we refer, for example, to Air Canada and the consolidation that has taken place in Imperial and Texaco, we see a reduction because it is in the same proportion of about 2,000 men and women who could lose their jobs on the basis of the government's action. The important thing about that, aside from-

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That's fear mongering.

subtopic: PETRO-CANADA PUBLIC PARTICIPATION ACT MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It is not fear mongering. It is a little bit better than having a monopoly on mistruths which is what you perpetrate all the time.
We can leave the nonsense to one side, and take a look at these men and women who are currently earning money, are not a drain on our economy and are contributing to our tax revenues through their contributions. Many of these people are going to be put at risk because the minister says the best thing to do is to go ahead and privatize.
We must keep in mind that everything that Petro-Canada has done has been accomplished without government funds. We are confused with the government's ambivalence. We must look at whether it is thinking about exporting jobs, whether it is sincere when it says that it wants to privatize everything, whether the marketplace should dictate all of the economy and whether it is honest when it says the government should not be involved in the marketplace and let business handle the marketplace itself.
Upon careful reflection, it appears that the government is not very consistent in its position. For example, if it is concerned about the amount of money that it put into areas of private enterprise, it is instructive to know that last year some $602 million in grants and cash payouts of taxpayers' money was given to private oil companies for exploration and development. Many of those recipients included some desperately poor multinationals. One example is Chevron. This is Chevron itself, not its sister companies and not its subsidiaries. It received a mere $7,358,254 to conduct those activities. Another example is Husky Oil. It received $4,582,523. Mobil Oil, one of the companies that is a partner in Hibernia, received $5,530,492. Texaco received $6,719,515. Amoco also received grants and moneys under CIDA in the amount of $2,585,062. These amounts do not include tax write-offs and other subsidies. These are strictly cash payments.
What I am trying to get across is that we have a government that says it cannot get involved in the activities of exploration and development, it cannot get involved in the marketplace, it must give this company an opportunity to handle things on its own, but it is willing to give out these millions of dollars to private oil companies to conduct exploration and development in Canada. What is so galling about all this is-I am not suggesting for a moment that that is not bad enough- there was a further $4,100,437 given to companies that did not have enough money to set up a subsidiary office in Canada. Therefore, the money was transferred directly to their offices in the United States.
For those of us who have difficulty comprehending how much money $600 million is, it represents a $10,000 tax on every little baby that was born last year. As soon as the doctor slapped the little baby on the buns, he said, "Here you are, wake up, you have a $10,000 debt to the oil companies, thanks to the Government of Canada."
October 29, 1990

Obviously the government has a problem in deciding which direction to turn. Privatization is seemingly inconsistent with other government decisions.
My colleague pointed out a few moments ago that in the area of oil and energy development, the government is willing to put up the $600 million that I just cited. Look at what else it does with respect to Elibernia. There is $1.6 billion in subsidies and loans to Hibernia and a further $1 billion in soft loans. I do not think its rationale for that was contested by many of us. At the outset I would like to put Petro-Canada in perspective. As with the 13 other Crown corporations that have been privatized by the government, particularly three of the larger ones such as Canadair, Teleglobe,
Government Orders
and Air Canada, I want to emphasize that Petro-Canada is a major Canadian corporation.
First, it is a Crown corporation and based on 1989 figures-I am using The Globe and Mail Report on Business of July, 1990, for my figures so they may differ slightly from some which have been used in this debate. I want to assure hon. members that the figures I am using have not been manufactured for me by any particular source, but they are independent public figures published in the leading business journal of the country.
The Report on Business states that Petro-Canada is the largest Crown corporation in terms of sales revenue at $5 billion. In terms of assets, it is the third largest Crown corporation with assets of $6.8 billion, ranking behind the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and behind Canadian National Railway.
It ranks third among Crown corporations in terms of profits and the figures that I have for its profits before extraordinary items are $85 million in 1989, well behind the CNR and Canada Post.
In one other measure, Petro-Canada fairs only seventh among Crown corporations and that is in terms of return on capital where it was listed at 7.8 per cent for 1989. By comparison, this key statistic for Canada Post was 9.68 per cent, and for the CNR it was 8.68 per cent. Ordinarily one would not be very impressed with any corporation that finished behind the CNR or Canada Post in terms of business performance. As we all know, those two traditional Crown corporations have for many years been financial millstones around the government's neck and it has been only in the last couple of years, under the direction of this government, that both those corporations have commenced to perform as legitimate profitable corporations.
To gain a full perspective about Petro-Canada, it is also necessary to compare it with one or two similar private companies in the integrated oils category. For example, Imperial Oil revenues are twice as large at $10 billion and Shell Canada at $5 billion is just about equal to Petro-Canada.
However, when it comes to profitability, the comparisons are not so favourable. Shell's profitability is three times greater for the same sales and Imperial's profitability is five times greater for twice the sales. In the critical category of return on capital, there is a remarkable demonstration of difference between the two well-

October 29, 1990
Government Orders
run private companies, each exceeding 15 per cent return on invested capital over a five-year period annually, whereas the Crown corporation, Petro-Canada, which is also a well-run company, shows only one-third that performance at 5.13 per cent annual return on capital over the five-year period.
I think that those are meaningful figures in this debate because we are talking about the basic philosophy of turning the public Crown corporation in a private enterprise direction.
The question naturally arises, particularly for those of socialist persuasion, why even think of doing such a thing? Is it not better, they ask, to keep the company in government hands on behalf of the people, rather than risk private enterprise initiative for that dirty word, profit? It seems to me the facts about return on capital firmly answer those questions. For some inexplicable and mystical reason, private corporations just seem to run a lot more efficiently and successfully than Crown companies. As I say, just note the difference in return on capital between Imperial and Shell at 15 per cent annually and Petro-Canada at just over 5 per cent, a three-to-one differential in performance.
One of the basic principles of the privatization process which is followed consistently from the government's agenda for economic renewal presented in 1984 is a market-oriented energy policy. It is based on the belief that the private sector, guided by efficiently functioning markets, is in the best position to make optimal decisions concerning energy consumption, production, and investment. Surely the stark reality of the numbers I have presented with regard to return on capital, particularly, help to confirm the basic truth of that principle. Somehow the private enterprise performer is almost always more efficient, more effective and more productive than the government-controlled company. One of the principles, one of the tenets in 1984 when this government commenced to restructure the country's economic framework was to enable Canadians to become more competitive generally in our efforts to meet the challenges of the emerging global marketplace.
Therefore, I strongly support this legislation which authorizes the sale of shares in Petro-Canada to the general public because I believe that direction will ultimately prove the best both for Petro-Canada and for the government representing all Canadians.
As Petro-Canada is gradually transformed to face both the opportunities and the disciplines of the private market system, I feel confident that its performance will emulate its major competitors because it already is a sound and solid corporation. I believe that privatization will make it perform even better.
There are obviously other reasons which strongly support this legislation. Petro-Canada needs increased capital to develop its oil and gas reserves. Since gaining a commercial mandate in 1985, Petro-Canada has become a major player in several energy megaprojects. It presently has the second largest proven reserves of oil and natural gas liquids in Canada and the fourth largest natural gas reserves of any company in the country.
It will take money, lots of it and much of it at very high risk to develop these reserves on a viable, profitable basis.

Mr. Speaker, Petro-Canada is one of hundreds of oil and gas companies operationg in that major field of activities. Let us keep that in mind. Petro-Canada accounts for roughly 6 per cent of exploration and development operations in Canada. Nor should we forget that the development of these resources requires a lot of capital.

The best way to raise that capital is through a public share issue where investment is made on the merits of the market system and not simply by tapping the federal treasury for huge new amounts that will reflect in higher taxes or a larger government deficit. That is where the moment of truth occurs in the enterprise process, when a corporation is compelled to demonstrate its plan for attracting capital and must do so in a highly competitive way. That is when the prospects for performance are evaluated in the context of the investment required and the test is whether or not the money is forthcoming.
Last, I support the legislation because state ownership of Petro-Canada is no longer necessary for the company to achieve public policy objectives, if it ever was required for that purpose. When Petro-Canada was created in the 1970s, the Liberal government of the day set three objectives for its public policy role on behalf of the people of Canada. First, it was to increase the petroleum supplies available and to increase exploration for new sources of oil and gas, especially in the frontier areas of Canada's coast and in the Arctic. Second, the company
October 29, 1990

was to provide a window on the oil and gas industry to help government formulate national energy policies. Third, the company was to act as Canada's agent in any negotiations with other states concerning energy supplies.
Looking back in history, we have all come to realize that government ownership of Petro-Canada is no longer required to achieve those public policy objectives. In fact, we have come to the realization that there is only one principal public policy objective in the energy sector. That is to establish the conditions in which the economic development of our energy resources can occur. There is now good reason to believe that privatization of Petro-Canada will better serve that major policy objective and will not put other energy policy objectives at risk through privatization.
For example, we now have a much clearer perspective on the extent of our frontier reserves and on their potential for development. We are confident that the private sector is the best approach there. The government has a variety of mechanisms to remain intimately informed about the industry, including the Petroleum Monitoring Agency, the Canada Oil and Gas Lands Administration and the National Energy Board. We do not need a major Crown corporation as a window on the industry at all.
If trading directly with other states becomes a requirement, there are other more direct options which the government can use. The capabilities and expertise exist in more than one government department: Energy, Mines and Resources for one and International Trade for another.
In summary, therefore, the original reasons for government ownership of Petro-Canada are no longer valid, and one wonders if they ever really were valid. It is tempting to draw a parallel between Petro-Canada and the infamous National Energy Program which was introduced to Canada by the Liberal government 10 years ago.

As business and political writer, Tom Kier-ans, said in his report on Business Magazine of July 1990:
Government Orders
"The National Energy Program was a reckless and thinly veiled experiment with a planned economy."
Even the energy minister of the day, the hon. Marc Lalonde, admitted that the National Energy Program was not about people, it was about power. Ottawa's aim was not simply to sustain and cushion eastern Canada against oil shocks, but rather as Kierans observed, "It was the intention of the federal government to recycle a large component of the huge energy price increase through its coffers so that it could both restructure the energy industry, and also redirect the industrial economy while increasing its federal control".
The government was basing its planning on estimates that oil prices would reach $80 per barrel. Some plan. Even though consumers would be paying a lot more for petroleum products, the oil and gas industry would be very prosperous, it contemplated, and government revenues would be so large that all of its social programs would be supported and the federal government would probably have no deficit.
