Mr. Speaker, talk about the GST and the burden which many people claim it will bring to Canadians. Can you imagine what the National Energy Program was designed and disguised to accomplish? It was to bleed us dry at $80 a barrel and that was the plan for this nation.
We all know what happened. Oil prices collapsed, and the planned economy collapsed with it. Unfortunately, however, many of the social contracts had already been put in place and much of the government spending was already under way. Today we see the result of massive deficits which were accumulated in the early 1980s, and the incestuous process of debt upon debt which became embedded in the system by the time the current government came to power in 1984.
To a considerable extent in this bill, Mr. Speaker, we see the distinctions here of political philosophy, and we saw them with the National Energy Program as well. We are confronted with some of the basic differences and political principle between a Liberal outlook that "government knows best, and does best", the Socialist outlook that "governments should own everything", and the

October 29, 1990
Government Orders
Conservative philosophy of "The market system does it best, let it work".
It is worth reviewing briefly again some of the main features of this government's energy policy which impact on the Petro-Canada bill. As emphasized at the start, we have implemented a market approach to energy policy in the belief that the private sector is by far the best vehicle to achieve Canada's energy goals.
Consistent with that philosophy, we have reformed regulations governing the energy sector, and have allowed prices to be set by market forces.
Of utmost importance, the government has negotiated secure access to the vast U.S.A. market for Canadian energy products via the free trade agreement. This historic move has created an atmosphere in which investment in this country is now again fostered, including foreign investment, while ensuring continued opportunities for Canadians to participate in the oil industry.
Shortly after taking office in 1984, this government dismantled that grand Liberal experiment in a planned economy called the National Energy Program. It was already even then dying of its own bureaucratic weight, and of the reality that the golden goal of $80 per barrel for oil was long a dream or a nightmare of the past. Unfortunately, a large part of Canada's financial stability collapsed in the ruins of the National Energy Program.
In 1985, the government gave Petro-Canada a commercial mandate, and it has commenced to make significant progress as one of Canada's largest integrated oil companies.
Now, by commencing to privatize Petro-Canada, the company will be given the freedom it requires to run its business on a market basis without the burdens imposed by government ownership, and with access to the private market for investors and operating partners.
Security of energy supply has always been a key component of Canadian energy policy, and this government has recognized that security can best be achieved by ensuring that Canada possesses a strong, diverse and growing energy sector. We have put in place policies to encourage the development of all economically viable forms of energy. Through regulatory reform and the removal of oppressive and discriminatory taxes, we have created the conditions which will enable the domestic oil industry to grow, and which will stimulate the exploration necessary for new reserves of oil and gas to serve the future.
Also, to encourage security of supply, Canada has established emergency procedures within our own domestic market to deal with possible shortages and has entered into emergency sharing procedures with our international energy agency partners in the event that physical shortages of oil should occur. That sort of condition is intensified in these days of crisis in the Persian Gulf.
Those are some of the key directions of Canada's energy policy. As I have said before, the privatization of Petro-Canada will not only serve those policies but it will bring many other benefits as well, both for the company and for the country.
By placing Petro-Canada on the same basis as its private sector competitors, we will increase the business potential which Petro-Canada will have to develop its assets and to acquire new ones.
Privatization will permit the company access to the full range of private sector financial markets and instruments, which will help it to build its business in a timely fashion.

Mr. Speaker, privatization will provide Petro-Canada management with the financial flexibility enjoyed by their competitors and give them ready access to new funds without adding a cent to the tax load of Canadians. By limiting the over-all participation of foreigners we can gain all these benefits while making sure that Petro-Canada remains under the control of Canadians.

Equally important, the financial resources of government will be relieved of such financial support and investment which truly does belong in the private sector, where the efficiencies of performance are so well demonstrated.
Last, privatization will remove the myth that government needs direct participation as an operator in the oil and gas business to achieve our public policy objectives. It has been clearly demonstrated in many ways that Petro-Canada is not, has not been for some time, and perhaps may not ever have been, an effective direct instrument of government energy policy. Like the National Energy Program, it has been a grand interventionist scheme going largely in the wrong direction and not
October 29, 1990

toward the destinations and goals which our country must find and obtain. Clearly, Petro-Canada does have a major role to play in the development of Canada's energy reserves, and I have utmost confidence that with its excellent workforce of almost 7,000 people and its outstanding management, Petro-Canada will play that role in extremely successful ways. Its future will be found, not as an instrument of government policy, but rather as an active and competitive private sector company in the forefront of the Canadian energy effort. It is in that manner, along with so many other dynamic enterprises on the Canadian energy scene that both the company and the country will be well served with efficient, effective, reliable and competitive energy supplies for decades to come.

Mr. Speaker, while the creation of Petro-Canada may be viewed as the product of an ideology, the decision to privatize flows from good old common sense.

Those are among the reasons, Mr. Speaker, why I strongly support Bill C-84 and the privatization of Petro-Canada Corporation.
Along with Canadair, TeleGlobe Canada, Air Canada, and with 10 other of those Crown corporations since 1984, a commitment has been fulfilled by this government, not an ideological commitment toward a planned economy but a common sense commitment in the best interests and best traditions of Canadian and Conservative directions.

Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman has covered a very wide horizon of issues in his question. I would like to respond to him very quickly.
The performance of the Irving company, both in petroleum and in other interests in New Brunswick, is a source of pride to all New Brunswickers. I would challenge him to put that question to his own NDP leader in New Brunswick. I believe that she would criticize him for making such an inference.
On the other question he raises about the management of Petro-Canada, I have said on two occasions in my address and once in answer to a question that I regard the management and the performance of Petro-Canada highly. In fact any Crown corporation that can show a profit at all is an exemplary organization. What the record shows is that if that company is put into the private market system, the chances are that it will emulate the performance of Imperial Oil and Shell, which will be to triple its present return on capital.
In closing, I would like to refer to the three major companies that have been discussed in terms of privatization prior to this bill. Canadair's sales have risen since privatization from $438 million to $800 million. Its employment has risen from 4,667 to 7,200. Air Canada's profit went from a loss of $22 million in 1985 to a profit of $36 million in 1989. In the case of Teleglobe, the demand for service is rising at the rate of 30 per cent annually. These are examples of what happens when we take government's burdensome ownership away from a corporation and put it into the private market system which serves all Canadians much better and in a far superior manner.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take part in this debate today with a sense of alarm that this government is going to privatize the institution we call Petro-Canada, a corporation that is already owned by Canadians. Now it is going to sell back to us something we already own.
The original purpose for the creation of Petro-Canada was to provide a window on the oil industry for Canadians and to explore for gas and oil in Canada's
Government Orders
frontiers. It did this very effectively until this government came to power and cancelled Petro-Canada's public policy role, telling the publicly owned company to behave just like any other private sector oil companies. Now look what has happened.
In 1984 we had approximately 5,800 oil wells drilled, completed, and brought into production in Canada. Last year there were 1,720 oil wells drilled and brought into production. This year, as of October 6, there were only 1,306 oil wells drilled and brought into production here in Canada. As of October 9, there were 306 oil drilling rigs in Canada that were down. They were not working. There were 23 rigs in the process of moving, and only 159 rigs actually drilling. Only one-third of the oil rigs in Canada are working at the present time when we are facing an energy crisis. So much for the private sector.
Just recently, James K. Gray, Executive Vice-President of Canadian Hunter Exploration Limited of Calgary, stated in a speech:
Our current supply of conventional crude oil is diminishing. As an explorationist I can assure you that there are still discoveries to be made, and it is crucially important that we be encouraged to explore. Nevertheless, trends indicate that conventional oil production will decline by over 20,000 barrels per day per year in Canada over the next 30 years, while demand is expected to increase by approximately 25,000 barrels per day per year over the same period. Our modest surplus of production will soon disappear.
That is from the oil industry itself telling us what is going to happen over the next few years.
I have further concern that it is not just happening in Canada. The decline in Canada will begin in 1991 to 1995 by about 10 per cent. During the period 1987 to 1990 production in the United States declined by about 25 per cent to 50 per cent. I should point out that crude oil in the United States now amounts to 41 per cent of its needs.
It is this type of lack of direction from this government that is putting Canada in another energy bind. Here we are going to privatize a public company that was set up to develop frontier lands at a time when we are coming into an energy crunch.
Petro-Canada stands as number two in terms of oil reserves. It stands as number two among all the companies. only exceeded by Imperial Oil. It stands as number two in gas reserves and as number four in gas production. It stands as number one in net land holdings in this nation. Petro-Canada has control of most land holdings,

October 29, 1990
Government Orders
or more control, than the other companies in Canada at the present time.
It was put there to fulfil a mandate, to do the exploration work in Canada's frontier. This government has cancelled that mandate.
Mr. Speaker, why has the private sector not picked up the challenge in the frontier lands and the offshore? Why has their exploration work dried up? It is because in a land as vast as ours and the harsh climates in our Arctic and the frontier, one needs incentives because the private sector is not going to do it. After this government deregulated the oil and gas industry and took away Petro-Canada's mandate, things have gone downhill ever since.
This is one of the reasons why Petro-Canada has not shown the same rate of return, because of the high-risk exploration it did on the frontiers. It probably has not yet got the return back from the oil pipelines built to service those wells.
It is only recently we have seen the price of natural gas change, and that is in response to the start of construction of the Mackenzie gas pipeline.
I think we should look at what has happened in Canada. First of all, last December, under the so-called free market system when we had a cold snap all of a sudden propane prices almost doubled. Propane is a by-product of the oil industry, bottled gas we call it, but it is really bottled propane. Many people have to rely on this for their heating and just recently the price has gone up again.
I had a constituent call me just a few days ago who has a fleet of school buses powered by propane. He called to tell me he was not sure whether he could continue to operate because of the current high price of propane. But the sad thing is there is no shortage of propane.
It is the private sector taking advantage of an energy shortage, not in Canada because these prices are set outside of Canada in Texas. An organization outside of our own country is really controlling our prices and determining what lies ahead. It is not much wonder we have problems in the Middle East when we have the type of chess games being played by the huge oil companies in wanting to ensure a supply of product to supply the world
from wherever they choose at whatever price they feel they should pay.
It is nothing new for the government to be subsidizing oil companies. Hibernia would never be developed without the $2.7 billion, I believe, of federal government backing that is going in there.
Time will tell whether or not any of that oil will ever benefit the Canadian people. We are putting out a tremendous amount of money to bring that onstream, but there is nothing in the agreement that says the oil has to be refined or sold in Canada. There is no long-term security of supply there for the Canadian people. When we look at the equal access that the Americans have to our energy supplies under the free trade agreement, it makes me wonder how this government could ever think of privatizing a corporation like Petro-Canada because it is our operation and it was established through Canadian taxpayers' money. Now the government has given it away and the Americans have equal access.
I think rather than privatizing Petro-Canada we should be going the other way. I think the mandate should be broadened and strengthened. We have diminishing reserves of conventional oil in Canada and the United States. We have tar sands oil but that is one of the most expensive to produce.
Rather than limiting its mandate, Petro-Canada should be expanded back to where it was at the time this government took office, with responsibilities on the frontier and the offshore, where the private sector does not want to venture because of the risk involved. We as Canadians need assured reserves. I think it should expand to include the development and use of renewable fuels. I am talking here about ethanol, for example. There is only one oil company among all those in Canada who is actually involved in this, and that was again with a level of government subsidy in terms of research and development.
I think we have to look very seriously at expanding the mandate of this Crown corporation. For example, there are millions of tonnes of grain stacked across the prairies that could be the source of a renewable fuel. It could account for up to 10 per cent of the automotive fuels used in this nation. Not only would it provide a market
October 29, 1990

for the millions of tonnes of grain that remain unsold, but it could provide a domestic market for between five and eight million tonnes of that grain. At the same time, it could clean up the environment.
The use of 10 per cent ethanol in an automotive fuel will lower the carbon dioxide emissions of those fuels by 10 per cent. That is the first benefit. It would also provide a means of getting rid of carbon dioxide emissions by the very fact that the growth of a plant itself removes carbon dioxide from the air. An acre of corn, wheat or barley will remove as much carbon dioxide from the air as an acre of forest. We are all concerned about the destruction of our forests, not only in Canada but in the Amazon rain forests and other countries of the world. So we could have a double-barrelled impact on pollution. I think the government should look very seriously at moving in this direction.
I am shocked to find out that the additive put in gasoline by oil companies at the present time in Canada to replace lead-and this took place a couple of years ago-is not allowed to be used in the United States. But it is manufactured there and sold to us, and here we are using it in our vehicles to further pollute the atmosphere.
The oxygen content of ethanol blend is almost twice that of other oxygenated fuel resulting in reduced carbon monoxide emissions. It could be as much as 25 per cent. I said 10 per cent previously, but it could be up to 25 per cent.
I should point out that currently the city of Toronto ranks as one of North America's worst cities in downtown carbon monoxide levels and most of this is from car exhausts.
Just this afternoon on the way to Ottawa, we landed at Toronto Island Airport. We circled out over Lake Ontario to come in for the approach to the landing. We looked at the cloud of haze lying over that city, and most of that at this time of year has to be automotive emissions.
This government has an opportunity to expand the mandate of this Crown corporation into the development of renewable fuels, which will benefit all Canadians and here it is going to sell it off to the private sector because it thinks it can do better. Yet when we examine the dismal record of what has happened in the Arctic in the last few years, and currently there are nine rigs in the Arctic, not one of them drilling at the present
Government Orders
time, or as I should say as of early October and late September.
I look at the record of what happens under privatization, and I have to look at the Polysar situation in the city of Sarnia. It was established in 1971 with $250 million worth of seed money. Once again, if it charged less than the other companies, it would have gone bankrupt and put itself out of business. Mr. Speaker, as you have just indicated, I only have five minutes to participate in this debate. That is not a lot of time to deal with a matter like the privatization of Petro-Canada, Bill C-84.
Let us be blunt about our language today in dealing with this bill, because there has been an awful lot of nonsense, most recently by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance, being spewed about this House.
We are not dealing with the privatization of Petro-Canada, a 15 per cent share offering. That is an unmitigated farce. The Government of Canada is selling off Petro-Canada lock, stock and barrel, 100 per cent. There is nothing in this bill that limits the share offering to 15 per cent. There is nothing to indicate it will only be a partial privatization. It is a full privatization. It is a giveaway of another national asset, but this government
October 29, 1990

lacks the courage or the integrity to say so. That is what is happening.
What is going on in Canada today with a government that languishes for the last five months at 15 per cent in the polls, that is despised in this country, is analogous to what is happening to Kuwait. There was not an invasion. There was a democratic election. However we have a regime in Kuwait today that knows it is not staying there for very long. While they are there, the people, the army of Iraq, the army of Saddam Hussein, is plundering Kuwait. They are taking away the furniture. They are taking away the wealth of the nation. They are stripping the assets of the nation. This government, at 15 per cent in the polls, knowing that at the next election it is finished, on behalf of is corporate friends in whose pockets it lives, is stripping away the assets of Canada. That is what is happening today.

This is the government that sold Route Canada, part of a Crown corporation, with all of the same rhetoric and rationale we heard today, to an individual who could not even qualify for a credit card.
My God, Mr. Speaker, is there no depth to depravity, the ideological foolishness of this party? Imagine selling a $35 million asset to a Canadian whose only qualification was his Tory membership cards because his credit cards had been cancelled. Can you believe it, Mr. Speaker?
That is the mentality of that party. It sold Air Canada. It was going to do great things in the marketplace. It was going to flourish. It was going to change the Crown corporation involvement and fly even higher. What has Air Canada done? It has laid off 3,000 employees and financially it is going down.
The Conservatives sold off Fisheries Products International. They were going to unshackle Fisheries Products International. It was going to fly in the corporate world and what has happened? Its shares have died down and we have a disaster, people bleeding left, right and centre, all over the place in the fishery.
Let us not waste time, in the few minutes we have left, with subtle language about the free market. The free market implies competition. That is what it means: competition. However, what is happening in Canada?

We have an incredibly concentrated energy sector, incredible concentration. That is not competition. That is capitalism, not free enterprise. That is the resources of the nation in the hands of a few for the benefit of the few and not for the nation as a whole. That is what we have. That is the creed of the Conservative Party as it strips away the assets of this nation.
We have a sector now that is dominated by U.S. interests and by U.K. interests or British interests. That is the reality and the one lever, if only this government had the guts to use it, and it hasn't. It is the one ability to have some say about the rip-offs that are currently going on at the gas pumps.
Look at this. Today, in The Ottawa Sun, third quarter profits of all of the oil companies in Canada have doubled, tripled, and quadrupled; amazing increases, and nothing but the sound of silence from members opposite.
It is time for these members, these plunderers of the national assets, to crawl out of their corporate pockets, go back and face their constituents, stand up for Canada, and protect the assets of this nation. The plunder must stop and stop soon.
